tagline.text: Philosophy that starts from the single person who must choose how to live.

overview.text: Existentialism is a loose family of ideas, not a tidy school. It starts from life as a person lives it, not from the detached, objective standpoint that much earlier philosophy preferred. A core idea: we make ourselves through our choices, and we are responsible for who we become.

sources.quote: certainly not a reference to a coherent system or philosophical school

burdened with the task of creating ourselves through our choices and actions

overview.text: Its ideas began to come together in the nineteenth century, with Søren Kierkegaard, from Denmark, and the German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche. The movement took off in mid-twentieth-century France, where Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir, two French philosophers and novelists, made it famous.

overview.text: Who counts? Of the major figures, only Sartre and Beauvoir called themselves existentialists. The French novelist Albert Camus and the German philosopher Martin Heidegger both rejected the label, but both are still counted in the tradition. Existentialists can be religious, like Kierkegaard, a Christian, or not, like Nietzsche and Sartre.

themes.title: Existence before essence
themes.summary: Your choices shape who you become, within real limits.

paragraphs.text: Sartre called it 'the first principle of existentialism': existence precedes essence. Your 'essence' would be a fixed nature that decides who you are; existentialists say we are not born with one. A person first 'turns up' and only afterwards defines himself, through choices made as life unfolds. How free are we, then? Early Sartre called our freedom 'absolute'. Later, he and others such as Beauvoir stressed that our social and historical situation limits it. But we can still question those limits, give them meaning and decide what to do with them. A strong craving, for example, does not force me to act on it.

sources.quote: the first principle of existentialism
not as a substance or thing with some pre-given nature
I do not out of necessity have to act on these desires
an account of “radical” or “absolute” freedom
It failed to engage the social, historical, and material conditions that invariably limit and constrain our freedom
had already been forwarded and developed by Beauvoir
our embodiment and spatiality, our creaturely appetites and desires, and the socio-historical context we find ourselves in

themes.title: Freedom and anxiety
themes.summary: You alone answer for your choices, and that can feel dizzying.

paragraphs.text: This makes us free, and responsible for what we make of ourselves. Take Sartre's example of a coward. Childhood or genes did not make him that way; he 'makes himself a coward' by his decisions. Realising this brings anxiety, which Kierkegaard called 'the dizziness of freedom'. Existentialists ask us to face this feeling, not run from it. It can shake us out of our comfortable routines.

themes.title: Authenticity versus the crowd
themes.summary: Going along with everyone feels comforting, but it lets us dodge our own choices.

paragraphs.text: Being authentic means being true to yourself. Existentialists criticise our habit of living by the rules and expectations of everyone around us. Heidegger's name for this crowd was 'the They': we enjoy, read and judge things as 'they' do. It feels like living well, but it hides our freedom from us.

paragraphs.text: Sartre and Beauvoir call this kind of self-deception 'bad faith'. It comes in two forms:

paragraphs.text: What authenticity looks like varies by thinker:

items: Kierkegaard: a passionate commitment that unifies a scattered life.
Nietzsche: creating your own values and saying yes to your whole life.
Heidegger: pulling your life together around what matters to you, while staying ready to let it go if your circumstances change.
Sartre and Beauvoir: facing your unsettled situation clearly and taking responsibility for what you do.

items: Nietzsche summed up the crisis as 'God is dead'. He did not mainly mean that there is no God. He meant that belief in the Christian God had become unbelievable, so the morality built on it would collapse. His answer: create your own values.

Camus called our situation 'the absurd', the clash between our 'wild longing for clarity' and 'the unreasonable silence of the world'. If life has no meaning, he asked, is it still worth living, or is suicide the answer? He said it is worth living: reject suicide and false hope, and live fully aware.
Beauvoir disagreed with calling life absurd: that would mean it can never have a meaning. Its meaning is never fixed, so we keep making it.

themes.title: My freedom needs yours
themes.summary: Other people can trap us as objects, yet my freedom depends on theirs.

paragraphs.text: Sartre and Beauvoir argued that we see ourselves through 'the look' of others, and that their gaze can turn us into objects. Sartre's example: you are peeping through a keyhole, lost in the scene. Suddenly you hear footsteps, and you feel shame as you see yourself as an object in someone else's eyes. Sartre's play No Exit sums this up in its famous line that hell is other people.

sources.quote: the look has the power to strip away my freedom and turn me into an object
we are asked to imagine that we are peeping through a keyhole
Suddenly, though, we hear footsteps, and we have an involuntary apprehension of ourselves as an object in the eyes of another
Hell is—other people

paragraphs.text: But there is a better way. Beauvoir's 'authentic love' nurtures the other person's freedom instead of possessing them. Why does my freedom need yours? If freedom is the core of what I am, it is the core of others too, so my freedom is bound up with yours. That is why we must help free each other, so that each of us can create ourselves. As Sartre put it, in wanting freedom 'we discover that it depends entirely on the freedom of others'.

sources.quote: authentic love
depends entirely on the freedom of others
I understand or see myself in the way that I do through “the look” (le regard) of the Other
it is invariably bound up in the freedom of others
we have a shared obligation to liberate or free each other so that we can create ourselves
When I acknowledge that freedom is my essence, I must also acknowledge that it is the essence of others

thinkers.name: Søren Kierkegaard
thinkers.summary: Søren Kierkegaard was born in Copenhagen in 1813 and wrote mostly in the 1840s, across philosophy, theology, psychology and social critique. He opposed building grand systems and is often called the 'father of existentialism', though SEP warns the label hides as much as it shows. He has often been cast as Hegel's great opponent, but recent scholars think his main target was certain Danish Hegelians.

thinkers.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
thinkers.summary: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher and cultural critic who published intensively in the 1870s and 1880s. He is famous for fierce attacks on traditional European morality and religion, often by exposing the hidden psychology behind received ideas. He also proposed new values he hoped would renew culture, and SEP's existentialism entry counts him among the movement's nineteenth-century pioneers.

key_ideas.text: 'God is dead': belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable, so the morality built on it is set to collapse.

thinkers.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
thinkers.summary: Jean-Paul Sartre was, with Simone de Beauvoir, the most popular voice of mid-twentieth-century French existentialism, and a novelist, playwright and public intellectual. His treatise Being and Nothingness (1943) is called the defining work of the movement, and his 1945 lecture Existentialism is a Humanism drew huge crowds. Later he tried to combine existentialism with Marxism.

key_ideas.text: Existence precedes essence: we turn up first and define ourselves afterward through our choices.
We are 'condemned' to be free: no fact about our situation fixes how we respond to it, so we are responsible.
Bad faith is self-deception: denying either our freedom or the facts of our situation.

thinkers.name: Simone de Beauvoir
thinkers.summary: Simone de Beauvoir was a philosopher, novelist, feminist and activist, and one of the major figures of post-war French existentialism. She is best known for The Second Sex (1949), her trailblazing work in feminist philosophy. She called herself an author rather than a philosopher, but scholarship has secured her place as a thinker in her own right, not merely Sartre's helper.

thinkers.name: Albert Camus
thinkers.summary: Albert Camus was a journalist, novelist, playwright and essayist who more than once denied being a philosopher. His Myth of Sisyphus sits squarely in the existentialist tradition, yet he denied being an existentialist and wrote against Kierkegaard, Jaspers and Heidegger. He won the Nobel Prize for literature in 1957 and died in a car accident in 1960.

intro.text: Existentialist ideas shaped existential psychotherapy, which aims to help people with questions such as meaning and the fear of death. Even thinkers whose views differed from the existentialists' took up these questions, such as the Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl, who created logotherapy, a therapy built around finding meaning.

practice.after: But choosing an adviser, Sartre said, is already a choice: you more or less know what they will say. His only reply was 'You are free, therefore choose, that is to say, invent.' One way to use his point: before your next hard choice, ask yourself why you picked the person you are asking, and what you already expect them to say. Whatever they say, the choice stays yours.

practice.text: Imagine a demon tells you that you must live this life again, 'innumerable times', with nothing new in it. Would you curse the demon? Or would you answer that you never heard anything more divine? If the thought took hold of you, Nietzsche wrote, it would transform you, or perhaps crush you. One influential reading treats it as a test of whether your life has been good, as a whole and in every detail. If that feels too big, one way in (our adaptation, not his): ask it of a single day first.
